passage:
I saw it behind the canteen, so I'm writing down what I remember. Three of Imran's friends were passing round a vape. One of them held it out. "Come on, one puff. Don't be boring." Imran smiled, not nervously as far as I could tell, though I can't say what was going on inside him. "I'm boring, fine," he said lightly. "Not for me." They pushed again and one rolled his eyes. Imran just shrugged, said, "I'm going to the library, coming?" and walked off. Two of them shouted something after him. I'm not sure whether he was upset. Later he sat with me at lunch and talked about cricket as if nothing had happened.

Parveen, Class 10

qa.q: Where did Parveen see the friends offering Imran a vape?
What does Imran's manner suggest about how he handled the pressure, and how sure can Parveen be?
qa.a: He smiled, spoke lightly and left, so he seems steady and unwilling to give in. But Parveen admits she can't know what he felt inside.

qa.q: What could Imran do if the friends keep pushing him?
qa.a: Keep his light, steady no, keep walking away and spend time with people who don't put his safety at risk. If it gets worse, he can tell an adult he trusts.

qa.q: How might one of the friends see Imran's refusal?
qa.a: Possibly as a small sting. One rolled his eyes and two shouted after Imran, so they may feel rejected or embarrassed that he wasn't swayed.

grounding: An observer describes a friend who is called boring, says a light steady no and leaves.

passage:
Monday. Behind the school canteen, Damini held out a small vape pen. "Everyone's trying it, Rashmi. Don't be so boring." Rashmi's stomach tightened. She laughed lightly. "Nah, not my thing." Damini rolled her eyes. The others giggled.
Wednesday. Damini tried again at the bus stop, with two other girls. "Just once. You're such a baby." This time Rashmi felt her face burn. She wanted to belong. She also wanted to breathe properly at her swimming trials. "Still no," she said steadily, and got on the earlier bus instead.
Friday. At lunch, Rashmi sat with the swimming team instead. Nobody offered her anything; they talked about the trials. That evening she told her mother about the week. Her mother said, "You kept yourself safe. That's what real strength looks like. And if they keep pushing, we'll talk to your class teacher together."
Damini stopped asking after that.

qa.q: What did Damini hold out behind the canteen?
How did Rashmi feel when Damini called her a baby at the bus stop?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and pressured, face burning, torn between wanting to belong and wanting to stay healthy.

qa.q: Which choices kept Rashmi safe, and why?
qa.a: She gave a light, steady no, left on the earlier bus, sat with friends who didn't pressure her, and told her mother.

qa.q: How might Damini see Rashmi's refusals?
qa.a: Damini seems annoyed at first, calling Rashmi boring, but eventually stops asking when Rashmi keeps refusing calmly.

grounding: A teen pushed by friends to try vaping says a light, steady no, leaves when needed and finds friends who don't cost her safety.

passage:
Leela, come here. I saw you with those boys behind the school wall. Let me tell you what happened to me.
When I was fifteen, in our Indore colony, my friends started bunking tuition to smoke beedis by the railway line. Every evening they'd say, "Come on, Darshan, don't be a scaredy-cat. It's just one."
I wanted to be with them so badly. They were my whole world. For two weeks I made excuses: headache, homework.
Then one evening they surrounded me and held one out. "Now or never."
That was the turning point. I laughed and said, "Never, then," and walked back home along the tracks. My heart was hammering all the way.
They teased me for a month. Then one of them, Sunil, quietly stopped going too. We became closer friends than ever.
Real friends don't make you pay with your health, beta. Your Darshan Chacha learned that by the railway line.

qa.q: Where did young Darshan's friends go to smoke?
How did young Darshan feel when his friends pressured him?
qa.a: Young Darshan felt torn and anxious, desperate to belong but not wanting to smoke, his heart hammering as he walked away.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Darshan gave a light but firm no, 'Never, then,' and walked away, which kept him safe and later led Sunil to follow.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt about Darshan's refusal?
qa.a: Sunil may have admired Darshan's courage and felt freer to stop too.

grounding: Darshan Chacha recalls friends pressuring him to smoke, saying a light but steady no, walking away and finding a truer friend.
